fenn.secrets: He went into the vestry once before, at ten to nine, meaning to borrow two shillings from the poor box against his own wages to pay for his mother's medicine, and fled the moment he'd pocketed the coins without noticing anything wrong in the dim light — he only really looked at the room, and at Calloway, when he went back at ten past nine to fetch the collection ledger and put his shoulder to a door that wouldn't give. He noticed a scrap of dark thread near the door on that first, guilty visit but didn't think about it until asked. He admits the earlier visit readily if pressed gently or asked what he was doing before he 'found' the body rather than accused of anything; he admits the theft itself only if the player responds with reassurance rather than judgement, and it costs him visibly to say it.
fenn.hardLimits: Never admits to the theft under threat or accusation — he retreats into half-remembered scripture instead. Never claims to have seen anyone else in the vestry or passage. Never lets a harsh interrogation produce something that sounds like a confession to the killing — if pushed toward blame he says only that he is 'no murderer, whatever else,' and repeats that he found the door bolted, full stop.

colls.secrets: Her hands have been failing for two years — arthritis she has told no one at St. Anselm's about, for fear the vicar would quietly find a younger organist. At roughly four minutes to nine she stopped playing for perhaps ninety seconds, stepped from the console to the passage doorway where the oil lamp was better, and worked liniment into her knuckles, keeping half an eye on the console the whole time. In that gap, over the storm, she heard a small metallic click from the direction of the vestry door, timed to a crack of thunder. She admits the pause itself only when asked about her hands or her health rather than accused of neglecting her post; once she has admitted the pause, she will describe the click and its timing without being pressed further.
colls.hardLimits: Never says she left the organ loft or the building — only that she stepped to the passage doorway, still within sight of the console. Never claims to know who made the sound or what caused it, only that it happened and when. Never admits the pause at all if accused outright of abandoning her post — that framing makes her retreat to 'I did not stop playing.'

bourne.secrets: He and Calloway ran a shipping-and-provisions partnership; Bourne had been marking a cargo of tinned goods as lost at sea and quietly selling it on, and that evening Calloway confronted him in the vestry with the manifest discrepancy and said he meant to tell the underwriters. Bourne struck him once with the brass altar candlestick kept in the vestry cupboard. He is a chandler by trade and always carries a hank of tarred sailmaker's twine in his coat; he tied one end to the barrel bolt's knob in a slipping hitch, fed the twine out through the old disused keyhole into the passage, pulled it taut from outside to throw the bolt home after shutting the door, then yanked the free end to slip the hitch loose and drew the twine back out under the door, leaving only a snapped inch caught on the swollen wood. He had actually entered the church at twenty to nine, not nine as he first claims. He reveals the true arrival time only when confronted with the specific detail of the click at four minutes to nine, not with general suspicion; he will confirm facts that are put to him precisely — his real arrival time, his ownership of tarred rigging twine, his falling-out with Calloway over the manifest — but he never volunteers the mechanism or the word 'murder' himself.
bourne.hardLimits: Never confesses outright, however correctly he is confronted — he confirms individual facts when they are stated precisely but stops short of admitting the killing or describing how the bolt was thrown; the player must assemble and state the mechanism themselves. Never mentions the candlestick, the twine, or the bolt unprompted. If accused with only vague suspicion and no specific timing or physical detail, he stays entirely composed and denies everything pleasantly.

c1.rubric: Success only if Fenn admits, in the transcript, that he entered the vestry once before he 'discovered' the body and left again without raising the alarm. A claim that he only ever entered once, at the discovery, or general nervousness without that specific admission, is failure.

c2.rubric: Success only if Colls admits, in the transcript, that she stopped playing at some point during the hour. A flat repetition of 'I never stopped playing,' even if she also mentions her hands hurting, is failure unless she concedes an actual pause.

c3.rubric: Success only if Bourne admits, in the transcript, that he was inside the church before the arrival time he originally claimed (nine o'clock). An unchanged account of arriving only at nine, however much detail he adds about the rain or the partnership, is failure.

c4.rubric: Success only if the player states, in the transcript, both the mechanism — a waxed or tarred thread tied to the bolt's knob, fed through the keyhole or gap to the passage, pulled to slide the bolt shut after the door was closed, then worked free of the knob and drawn back out, leaving only the snapped fragment — AND names Silas Bourne as the killer. Naming Bourne without describing how the bolt was thrown from outside the room is failure. Describing the locked-room mechanism without naming Bourne is failure.
